principles: Keep the supported serve surface honest: if a flag is not documented, it should not remain as hidden compatibility.
Make the smallest possible code change that preserves the documented lattice serve, --dev, and --port behavior.
Use regression coverage that is cheap to run and hard to forget so the hidden aliases do not quietly return.
drivers: The docs and user prompts already advertise only the supported serve surface.
The current dev-cli launcher still has direct --web / --cli branches, so the source and docs are already drifting.
The repo already has npm run test:entrypoints, which can host a narrow launcher-contract guard without inventing a new test harness.

options.name: A: Delete the legacy alias branches and add a source-level entrypoint regression check
pros: Smallest change that removes the hidden compatibility path.
Leaves the documented serve behavior untouched.
A root entrypoint smoke can fail fast if the aliases return.
cons: Any private caller of --web or --cli loses that hidden behavior.
The guard is source-level plus smoke-based, not a dedicated runtime parser test.

options.name: B: Keep the aliases but leave them undocumented
pros: Preserves old ad-hoc callers if they still exist.
Avoids touching the launcher code path.
cons: Keeps the contract drift alive and leaves a hidden feature in the codebase.
Does not solve the maintenance problem the user is explicitly asking to remove.
Future readers still have to reason about dead compatibility code.

options.name: C: Remove the aliases and add an explicit unsupported-flag error
pros: Makes unsupported flags obvious to anyone who still tries them.
Prevents silent no-op behavior for old callers.
cons: Larger user-visible behavior change than requested.
Adds a branch that is not needed for the documented surface.
Could break ad-hoc private scripts more sharply than a simple cleanup.

chosen: A: Delete the legacy alias branches and add a source-level entrypoint regression check
rationale: This option removes the hidden compatibility path with the least surface area while keeping the supported serve flow unchanged and giving us a cheap guard against reintroducing the aliases.

preMortem.scenario: An internal script still passes --web or --cli after the cleanup.
preMortem.trigger: The script was copied from an old note or from memory, not from the current docs.
preMortem.consequence: The launcher no longer enters that hidden branch, so the caller may lose the expected extra behavior.
preMortem.mitigation: Confirm there are no in-repo callers, keep the docs/README surface clean, and make the entrypoint smoke fail if the aliases are reintroduced.

preMortem.scenario: The cleanup accidentally changes the actual serve startup behavior.
preMortem.trigger: While deleting the alias checks, the core spawn or vite startup logic gets edited by mistake.
preMortem.consequence: lattice serve no longer starts the same documented set of processes.
preMortem.mitigation: Limit edits to the alias branch and the regression check, then run build + entrypoint smoke before closing the story.

preMortem.scenario: A future refactor reintroduces the aliases in another file or path.
preMortem.trigger: Someone adds a new compatibility shortcut or copies the old behavior into another launcher helper.
preMortem.consequence: The hidden contract drifts back even though this cleanup shipped.
preMortem.mitigation: Keep the regression check in the root entrypoint test path and review the launcher source for any reappearance of --web / --cli.
